chapterTitle: Introduction to C# Scripting in Unity: Variables and Basic Logic

screens.title: Intro to C# Scripting in Unity
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter opens the door to scripting in Unity using C-sharp. You'll learn why Unity uses C-sharp, how scripts become the behavior of GameObjects, and how the MonoBehaviour base class gives scripts access to the engine. We will create a script asset, attach it to a cube, and observe how Start and Update control one-time initialization versus per-frame logic. You will also learn to declare variables like integers, floats, strings, and booleans, expose values to the Inspector with public fields, and use the print-to-console function for debugging. Finally, we'll demonstrate safe movement using the frame-time multiplier so motion stays consistent across machines. These skills matter because they transform static scenes into interactive worlds; variables let you parameterize behavior and the Start/Update lifecycle makes scripts react at the right times. As an example use case, you'll make a cube that greets the console, moves forward at a controllable speed, and rotates conditionally. Keep an eye out for common beginner pitfalls, like forgetting the float suffix or spamming the console from Update. Ready to turn static objects into behavior? Let's explore the specific topics you will master next.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Introduction to C# Scripting
Intro to C# Scripting in Unity
Variables, lifecycle methods, debugging, and basic movement
Why this chapter matters
Scripts are the behavior layer. Learning to structure simple scripts, expose variables, and use the engine's timing is essential for every interactive project.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will do four practical things. First, you will explain why Unity uses C-sharp and how scripts become components that drive GameObject behavior. This matters because understanding the role of code helps you decide where to place logic. Second, you will create a C-sharp script, name the class to match the file, and attach it to a GameObject so the engine runs your code. Third, you will use the Start and Update lifecycle methods correctly: put one-time setup in Start and per-frame logic in Update while knowing when to prefer FixedUpdate for physics. Fourth, you will declare common variable types — integer, float, string, and boolean — expose public fields to the Inspector, and use Debug. Log to print useful runtime information. Each objective includes hands-on practice so you gain muscle memory. These skills combine to let you make objects react, move, and report their state. As you work, check for common mistakes like missing the float suffix or misplacing Debug. Log calls in Update and practice fixing them.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills and Why They Matter
screens.narratorSegment: Let's expand on the practical skills you'll practice while learning. First, creating scripts and attaching them lets you iterate quickly; you can change parameters in the Inspector instead of re-editing code. For example, by declaring a public float speed you can try different movement rates without recompiling. Second, Start and Update split responsibilities: initialization and continuous updates. This reduces bugs — initialization code won't run every frame and per-frame work is kept lean. Third, Debug. Log is your immediate feedback loop. Use it to confirm values at startup or after key events, but avoid logging inside tight per-frame loops because it floods the Console and slows debugging. Fourth, understanding Time. deltaTime guards against frame-rate dependent behavior. Multiplying by this frame-time value yields consistent motion across machines. Practice these skills in small steps: expose a variable, change it in the Inspector, log its value at Start, then observe movement with and without Time. deltaTime to hear the difference. These exercises directly translate into more stable and tunable gameplay.

screens.title: C# and MonoBehaviour — The Script as a Component
screens.narratorSegment: Unity uses C-sharp as its primary scripting language because it is object-oriented and integrates with the engine through types and methods Unity expects. A Unity script file becomes a class; when that class inherits from MonoBehaviour, the engine can attach instances of it to GameObjects as components. That inheritance is more than a label — it provides lifecycle callbacks like Start and Update, access to engine APIs such as transform and Time, and the ability to enable or disable the component. Concretely, when you write public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour, Unity knows how to create that component, serialize its public fields for the Inspector, and call its message methods each frame. An example: a component that implements Start can initialize health or print a greeting exactly once, while Update is repeatedly called to move the object. A common misconception is to think MonoBehaviour is optional; without it, your class cannot be attached to a GameObject or receive Unity messages. As a quick practice, create a new script, name the class to match the file, inherit from MonoBehaviour, and verify that the Inspector shows the script component when attached. That confirms the connection between C-sharp classes and GameObject behavior.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: MonoBehaviour is the base class that lets your C-sharp class become a component attached to GameObjects and receive lifecycle calls.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › C# & MonoBehaviour
What MonoBehaviour gives you
  • Lifecycle messages like Start and Update for initialization and per-frame behavior.
  • Access to Unity APIs such as transform, gameObject, and Time.
  • Serialization of public fields so values appear in the Inspector for tuning.
Concrete example
Create a class named CubeMover that inherits from MonoBehaviour. Attach it to a Cube GameObject and watch Unity call Start once and Update each frame.
Key Takeaway

Without inheriting from MonoBehaviour, a class cannot be attached as a component or receive Unity's message callbacks.

Boilerplate
// Example script created by Unity
using UnityEngine;

public class CubeMover : MonoBehaviour
{
    // Start is called before the first frame update
    void Start()
    {
        Debug.Log("Hello, Unity Bootcamp!");
    }

    // Update is called once per frame
    void Update()
    {
        // Movement and per-frame logic go here
    }
}
Note: naming the class to match the file is a convention that avoids confusion and ensures the engine references the correct type.

screens.title: Create and Attach a Script
screens.narratorSegment: Creating and attaching a script is a simple process you will repeat often. First, organize your Project window by making a Scripts folder. This keeps code centralized and easy to find. Second, right-click inside that folder, choose Create, then C-sharp Script, and give it a descriptive name such as CubeController. Naming matters: match the file name to the class name that appears inside the script to avoid mismatches. Third, open the script with your configured IDE. Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code will show the boilerplate with the using statements, the class declaration, and empty Start and Update methods. Fourth, edit the class to add public fields or methods. Fifth, save and return to Unity; drag the script onto the GameObject in the Hierarchy or Inspector. Unity will add the script as a component and serialize public fields so they appear in the Inspector. A common mistake is forgetting to save the script before expecting changes to appear in Unity, or renaming the file without updating the class name, which causes compile errors. Practicing this sequence builds a reliable edit-run-debug loop you will use in every Unity project.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Create & Attach Script
Steps to create and attach
1. Organize
Create a Scripts folder in the Project window for clarity.
2. Create
Right-click → Create → C-sharp Script and name it meaningfully, e.g., CubeController.
3. Edit
Double-click to open in your IDE and add fields or logic.
4. Save
Save changes so Unity compiles and the Inspector reflects new fields.
5. Attach
Drag the script onto a GameObject to add it as a component.
6. Inspect
Adjust public fields in the Inspector and run the Scene.
Common mistakes
  • Renaming the file but not the class — causes compile errors.
  • Not saving the script before returning to Unity — changes won't appear.
Pro Tip

Use a dedicatedScripts folder and consistent naming conventions to avoid confusion while the project grows.

screens.title: Start() vs Update()
screens.narratorSegment: Start and Update are two of Unity's most important message methods. Start runs exactly once when the script instance becomes enabled, just before the first frame where Update could run. Use Start for initialization: setting initial positions, computing references, or printing a single welcome message. Update runs every frame and is where you put continuous checks, input polling, and movement code. Because Update is called based on frame rate, you must be mindful about performance and avoid expensive operations inside it. A common beginner error is to put one-time setup inside Update, which wastes C P U and can cause logic to execute repeatedly. Another important contrast is with FixedUpdate and LateUpdate: physics-related updates should use FixedUpdate to align with the physics timestep, and camera-follow logic often benefits from LateUpdate to run after other objects moved. For example, put Debug. Log in Start if you want one message; putting Debug. Log in Update will spam the Console each frame. This distinction keeps initialization separate from ongoing behavior and helps you write predictable, performant code. Start() vs Update() means start is for once-only initialization, update is for per-frame continuous logic; choose the right method to avoid wasted work or inconsistent behavior.. In practical terms, when initialization runs and when per-frame logic executes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Start() vs Update()
Start()
Runs once when the script is enabled. Ideal for initialization and one-time setup.
Example
Log a greeting or set starting hit points so those values are ready before gameplay begins.
Common Mistake

Placing initialization in Update results in repeated work and unexpected side effects.

Update()
Called once per frame. Use for input checks, movement, animation triggers, and non-physics continuous work.
Example
Poll for player input, move objects, or evaluate conditions each frame. Multiply time-dependent changes by Time.deltaTime for consistent motion.
Pro Tip

Keep Update efficient; expensive calls should be cached or moved to less frequent intervals.

screens.title: Debug.Log and the Console
screens.narratorSegment: Debugging with console output is one of the fastest ways to understand runtime behavior. In Unity, the print-to-console function prints messages to the Console window. Use it in Start to confirm initial values or in response to events to trace behavior. For example, logging the value of a public string from Start helps confirm that Inspector-assigned values are flowing into the script. However, logging in Update or tight loops can flood the console, making it hard to find useful messages and slowing down your editor. A good practice is to log high-level events, conditional states, and values you actually need to inspect. When a message is no longer useful, remove or comment out the call. Another helpful pattern is to include context in the message: include the GameObject's name and the variable value so the log is self-describing. Debug. Log is not a substitute for proper testing or breakpoints, but it offers immediate visibility into what the script does at runtime. Use it judiciously and pair it with Inspector checks for efficient debugging. Debug.Log and the Console means use debug.log for targeted checks and avoid placing it inside every frame to prevent console spam and slowdowns.. In practical terms, use console output for diagnosis, and avoid common pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Debug.Log & Console
When and how to log
  • Log in Start for initial values you want to confirm once.
  • Log on important events or state changes rather than every frame.
  • Include context like the object name and variable value so logs are self-explanatory.
Example message pattern
Include variable names and values, for example: "PlayerName is: Cohortia, HP: 90" so you can spot the exact state in the Console.
Avoid this
Putting Debug.Log inside Update without conditions will print every frame and quickly overwhelm the Console.
Key Takeaway

Use targeted logs and remove them when no longer needed to keep the Console useful and performant.

screens.title: Variables: int, float, string, bool
screens.narratorSegment: Variables are named storage locations for data. In C-sharp you declare their type explicitly. An integer stores whole numbers and is written as int. A float stores decimal numbers and requires an f suffix for literals, like 3.5f. Strings hold text and booleans represent true or false. You can declare variables inside your class but outside methods to make them fields. When you mark a field public, Unity serializes it and shows it in the Inspector so you can tweak it without changing code. For instance, public float moveSpeed = 5.0f; allows designers to tune movement speed directly from the Editor. Private fields do not appear in the Inspector by default. Use Debug. Log in Start to confirm that Inspector-assigned values were applied at runtime. A concrete example: declare public string greetingMessage = "Hello from the moving cube!" and then log it during Start to verify. A common beginner error is forgetting the f suffix for float literals or mixing up case in names since C-sharp is case-sensitive. Naming and visibility choices help you separate internal state from tunable parameters.

keyIdea.title: Variable basics
keyIdea.text: Declare typed fields, use public to expose them to the Inspector, and remember float literals need an f suffix.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Variables
Common types
  • int — whole numbers, e.g., int score = 100;
  • float — decimal numbers, e.g., float speed = 5.5f;
  • string — text, e.g., string name = "Cohortia";
  • bool — true or false, e.g., bool canMove = true;
Inspector visibility
Public fields appear in the Inspector. Private fields do not unless you use attributes, which you'll learn later.
Code example
using UnityEngine;

public class CubeMover : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float moveSpeed = 5.0f; // editable in Inspector
    public string objectName = "My Awesome Cube";
    private int hitPoints = 100; // internal state
    private bool canMove = true;

    void Start()
    {
        Debug.Log("My object's name is: " + objectName);
    }
}
Remember: floats need the f suffix on literals and C-sharp is case-sensitive.

screens.title: Public vs Private Fields and the Inspector
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between public and private fields affects encapsulation and workflow. Public fields are serialized and appear in Unity's Inspector, which is excellent for designers and rapid tuning. For example, a public float movementSpeed can be adjusted in the Editor without touching code. Private fields remain internal to the class and are not shown in the Inspector by default, which protects internal state such as a private int hitPoints. A best practice is to expose fields that represent tunable parameters and keep implementation details private. This reduces accidental changes and clarifies what other developers or designers should modify. A common misconception is that everything should be public for convenience — this creates brittle designs where internal state can be changed from outside in unexpected ways. If you need Inspector exposure for a private field, Unity provides serialization attributes, but for now use public for tuning and private for internal counters or flags. As you build components, think about the A P I your component presents to the Editor: expose what needs tuning, hide what should stay controlled by code. Public vs Private Fields and the Inspector means expose tunable parameters as public fields and keep internal state private to maintain clean component apis and avoid accidental edits.. In practical terms, when to expose a field and when to keep it internal. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Public vs Private
Public fields
Appear in the Inspector and are great for tuning values like speed, health, and messages.
Example
public float movementSpeed = 3.0f;
Private fields
Remain internal and protect implementation details like runtime counters and flags.
Example
private int hitPoints = 100;
When to use public
Tunable parameters and values designers should edit from the Editor.
When to use private
Internal state and implementation details that should not be exposed.
Misconception
Making everything public for convenience leads to fragile components and accidental edits.

screens.title: Movement with Time.deltaTime
screens.narratorSegment: Frame-rate independence is essential for predictable motion. Time. deltaTime provides the time in seconds since the last frame, and multiplying your speed by this value ensures that movement distances scale with elapsed time rather than frames. Without this multiplier, an object moves faster on high-frame-rate machines and slower on low-frame-rate machines. Consider transform. Translate(0, 0, moveSpeed * Time. deltaTime); with moveSpeed set to units per second — each frame you move by the small fraction for that frame's duration. A practical example: set moveSpeed to three units per second and observe the cube move the same distance whether the frame rate is thirty or one hundred frames per second. A common mistake is forgetting the f suffix on float literals or performing time-dependent math without Time. deltaTime in Update. For physics-based movement, FixedUpdate uses fixed timesteps, but for simple transform movement Update with Time. deltaTime is appropriate. Always think in units per second when designing movement parameters, and log distances at startup to confirm your expectations. Movement with Time.deltaTime means multiply speed by time.deltatime so movement represents units per second instead of units per frame.. In practical terms, make movement frame-rate independent using the frame time multiplier. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › CubeController Walkthrough
Full script
using UnityEngine;

public class CubeController : MonoBehaviour
{
    // Public variables appear in the Inspector!
    public float movementSpeed = 3.0f;
    public string greetingMessage = "Hello from the moving cube!";
    public bool canRotate = true;

    private int rotationDirection = 1;

    void Start()
    {
        Debug.Log(greetingMessage);

        if (canRotate)
        {
            Debug.Log("This cube is ready to spin!");
        }
        else
        {
            Debug.Log("This cube prefers to stay still.");
        }
    }

    void Update()
    {
        transform.Translate(0, 0, movementSpeed * Time.deltaTime);

        if (canRotate)
        {
            transform.Rotate(0, 30 * rotationDirection * Time.deltaTime, 0);

            if (Time.time > 5 && rotationDirection == 1)
            {
                rotationDirection = -1;
                Debug.Log("Changing rotation direction!");
            }
            else if (Time.time > 10 && rotationDirection == -1)
            {
                rotationDirection = 1;
                Debug.Log("Changing rotation direction again!");
            }
        }
    }
}

movementSpeed and canRotate are tunable values in the Inspector.
Rotation logic
rotationDirection flips based on Time.time to demonstrate state changes over time.

screens.title: Beginners' Pitfalls and How to Fix Them
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners commonly encounter a few recurring issues. First, forgetting the f suffix on float literals like 5.0f generates a compile error; C-sharp treats plain decimals as double by default. The fix is to add an f suffix or explicitly cast. Second, C-sharp is case-sensitive: Debug. Log must match the exact casing. Using debug. log will not compile because it does not match the A P I. Third, placing Debug. Log inside Update can flood the Console every frame. Limit logging to startup, events, or conditional states to keep the Console useful. Fourth, renaming a script file without updating the class name inside it causes compile-time mismatches; always keep the file name and class name aligned. Fifth, performing physics movement in Update can result in unstable physics behavior; prefer FixedUpdate for physics-controlled Rigidbody movement. Each mistake has a straightforward fix: read error messages, save before returning to Unity, and test small changes iteratively. Developing the habit of small, repeatable edit-run-observe cycles and reading the Console output will turn these mistakes into fast learning opportunities. This chapter opens the door to scripting in Unity using C-sharp. You'll learn why Unity uses C-sharp, how scripts become the behavior of GameObjects, and how the MonoBehaviour base class gives scripts access to the engine. We will create a script asset, attach it to a cube, and observe how Start and Update control one-time initialization versus per-frame logic. You will also learn to declare variables like integers, floats, strings, and booleans, expose values to the Inspector with public fields, and use the print-to-console function for debugging. Finally, we'll demonstrate safe movement using the frame-time multiplier so motion stays consistent across machines. These skills matter because they transform static scenes into interactive worlds; variables let you parameterize behavior and the Start/Update lifecycle makes scripts react at the right times. As an example use case, you'll make a cube that greets the console, moves forward at a controllable speed, and rotates conditionally. Keep an eye out for common beginner pitfalls, like forgetting the float suffix or spamming the console from Update. Ready to turn static objects into behavior? Let's explore the specific topics you will master next.

By the end of this chapter you will do four practical things. First, you will explain why Unity uses C-sharp and how scripts become components that drive GameObject behavior. This matters because understanding the role of code helps you decide where to place logic. Second, you will create a C-sharp script, name the class to match the file, and attach it to a GameObject so the engine runs your code. Third, you will use the Start and Update lifecycle methods correctly: put one-time setup in Start and per-frame logic in Update while knowing when to prefer FixedUpdate for physics. Fourth, you will declare common variable types — integer, float, string, and boolean — expose public fields to the Inspector, and use Debug. Log to print useful runtime information. Each objective includes hands-on practice so you gain muscle memory. These skills combine to let you make objects react, move, and report their state. As you work, check for common mistakes like missing the float suffix or misplacing Debug. Log calls in Update and practice fixing them.

Let's expand on the practical skills you'll practice while learning. First, creating scripts and attaching them lets you iterate quickly; you can change parameters in the Inspector instead of re-editing code. For example, by declaring a public float speed you can try different movement rates without recompiling. Second, Start and Update split responsibilities: initialization and continuous updates. This reduces bugs — initialization code won't run every frame and per-frame work is kept lean. Third, Debug. Log is your immediate feedback loop. Use it to confirm values at startup or after key events, but avoid logging inside tight per-frame loops because it floods the Console and slows debugging. Fourth, understanding Time. deltaTime guards against frame-rate dependent behavior. Multiplying by this frame-time value yields consistent motion across machines. Practice these skills in small steps: expose a variable, change it in the Inspector, log its value at Start, then observe movement with and without Time. deltaTime to hear the difference. These exercises directly translate into more stable and tunable gameplay.

Unity uses C-sharp as its primary scripting language because it is object-oriented and integrates with the engine through types and methods Unity expects. A Unity script file becomes a class; when that class inherits from MonoBehaviour, the engine can attach instances of it to GameObjects as components. That inheritance is more than a label — it provides lifecycle callbacks like Start and Update, access to engine APIs such as transform and Time, and the ability to enable or disable the component. Concretely, when you write public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour, Unity knows how to create that component, serialize its public fields for the Inspector, and call its message methods each frame. As a quick practice, create a new script, name the class to match the file, inherit from MonoBehaviour, and verify that the Inspector shows the script component when attached. That confirms the connection between C-sharp classes and GameObject behavior.

A common mistake is forgetting to save the script before expecting changes to appear in Unity, or renaming the file without updating the class name, which causes compile errors. Practicing this sequence builds a reliable edit-run-debug loop you will use in every Unity project.

Start and Update are two of Unity's most important message methods. Start runs exactly once when the script instance becomes enabled, just before the first frame where Update could run. Use Start for initialization: setting initial positions, computing references, or printing a single welcome message. Update runs every frame and is where you put continuous checks, input polling, and movement code. Because Update is called based on frame rate, you must be mindful about performance and avoid expensive operations inside it. A common beginner error is to put one-time setup inside Update, which wastes C P U and can cause logic to execute repeatedly. Beginners commonly encounter a few recurring issues. First, forgetting the f suffix on float literals like 5.0f generates a compile error; C-sharp treats plain decimals as double by default. The fix is to add an f suffix or explicitly cast. Second, C-sharp is case-sensitive: Debug. Log must match the exact casing. Using debug. log will not compile because it does not match the A P I. Third, placing Debug. Log inside Update can flood the Console every frame. Limit logging to startup, events, or conditional states to keep the Console useful. Fourth, renaming a script file without updating the class name inside it causes compile-time mismatches; always keep the file name and class name aligned. Fifth, performing physics movement in Update can result in unstable physics behavior; prefer FixedUpdate for physics-controlled Rigidbody movement. Each mistake has a straightforward fix: read error messages, save before returning to Unity, and test small changes iteratively. Developing the habit of small, repeatable edit-run-observe cycles and reading the Console output will turn these mistakes into fast learning opportunities. Keep these three ideas at hand as you write your first Unity scripts. First, C-sharp classes that inherit from MonoBehaviour become components attached to GameObjects and receive lifecycle calls like Start and Update. This connection is what makes code drive behavior in your scenes. Second, use public fields to expose tunable parameters in the Inspector and private fields for internal state. This separation keeps your component A P I clear and reduces accidental edits. Third, always think in units per second when moving objects: multiply movement by Time. deltaTime in Update to ensure consistent motion across different frame rates. These simple rules prevent many beginner issues and make your components predictable, tunable, and robust.
